aliases: Theory of functionals and linear operators

milestones.label: Volterra introduces functions that depend on other functions
milestones.work: Volterra, Sopra le funzioni che dipendono da altre funzioni, Rend. Accad. Lincei (4), 1887
milestones.description: Volterra's note defined quantities depending on a whole function, the notion later called a functional.

evidence.claim: zbMATH lists a 1887 Volterra paper on functions depending on other functions in the Lincei Rendiconti.
Wikipedia credits Volterra with the general concept of a functional in 1887.

milestones.note: MacTutor says Volterra conceived the idea in 1883 (a private precursor, not dated by a publication).

milestones.label: Volterra's functional calculus applied to Hamilton-Jacobi theory
milestones.work: Volterra, functional calculus papers, c. 1890
milestones.description: Volterra used functionals to extend the Hamilton-Jacobi integration theory of dynamics to other problems of mathematical physics.

evidence.claim: MacTutor states that in 1890 he showed his functional calculus extends the Hamilton-Jacobi theory to other physics problems.

milestones.note: Year taken from a biography; the specific 1890 paper was not identified.

milestones.label: Fredholm's theory of a class of functional equations
milestones.work: Fredholm, Sur une classe d'equations fonctionnelles, Acta Math. 27, 1903
milestones.description: Fredholm solved integral equations by the determinant method, giving the model for treating them as infinite linear systems.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Acta Mathematica 27, pp. 365-390, 1903.
MacTutor remembers Fredholm for integral equations and spectral theory.

milestones.label: Frechet's thesis on the functional calculus and abstract spaces
milestones.work: Frechet, Sur quelques points du calcul fonctionnel, Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo 22, 1906
milestones.description: Frechet's thesis introduced metric spaces and an axiomatic setting for analysis on spaces of functions, built on ideas of Hadamard and Volterra.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Rendiconti del Circolo Matematico di Palermo 22, pp. 1-72, 1906.
MacTutor describes the 1906 thesis as introducing metric spaces from the ideas of Hadamard and Volterra.

milestones.label: Hadamard's lectures introduce the noun 'functional'
milestones.work: Hadamard, Lecons sur le calcul des variations, 1910
milestones.description: Hadamard's book fixed the word 'functional' for a function of a function, replacing Volterra's own terminology.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive catalogue record for the 1910 first volume, collected by Frechet.
MacTutor says he introduced the word functional in this 1910 book.
Wikipedia dates the noun usage to Hadamard's 1910 book.

milestones.note: This names the object (functional), not the field; see the Levy 1922 milestone for the field's name.

milestones.label: Banach's thesis on operations in abstract sets
milestones.work: Banach, Sur les operations dans les ensembles abstraits et leur application aux equations integrales, Fund. Math. 3, 1922
milestones.description: Banach defined complete normed spaces and proved the contraction principle, launching the Polish school of linear operator theory.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Fundamenta Mathematicae 3, pp. 133-181, 1922.
MacTutor says this thesis is sometimes said to mark the birth of functional analysis.

milestones.label: Levy's 'Lecons d'analyse fonctionnelle'
milestones.work: Levy, Lecons d'analyse fonctionnelle, Gauthier-Villars, 1922
milestones.description: The earliest title found that uses the phrase for the field, a course reflecting Hadamard's school of nonlinear functionals.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record for Levy's Lecons d'analyse fonctionnelle, 1922.

milestones.note: Earliest title use of the phrase was not established; 1922 is the earliest found in a zbMATH search, so earlier uses are possible.

milestones.label: Banach's treatise on linear operators
milestones.work: Banach, Theorie des operations lineaires, Warsaw, 1932
milestones.description: The first monograph presenting linear operators on Banach spaces as a unified theory.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record for Banach, Theorie des operations lineaires, 1932.
Internet Archive scan listed under 1932.

notes: Sources: Wikipedia Functional_analysis; MacTutor biographies of Volterra, Hadamard, Frechet, Fredholm, Banach, Hilbert. Hilbert's integral-equation communications began in 1904 (not independently checked here); only the 1906 fourth communication and the 1910/1912 book were confirmed in zbMATH, so it is kept in people, not milestones. Riesz 1910 (Math. Ann. 69, Crossref 10.1007/BF01457637, L^p spaces) and Hadamard's 1903 note on functional operations (not found in zbMATH) were left out. Summary says 'fusion of analysis, algebra, topology'; the sources support abstract-space axiomatics (Frechet) rather than a single fusion date. Volterra priority: 1887 (publication) vs 1883 (MacTutor's idea). No MSC/journal institution milestone attempted (MSC 46 not verified).

milestones.label: Volterra: functions that depend on other functions
milestones.work: Volterra, Sopra le funzioni che dipendono da altre funzioni, Rend. Accad. Lincei (4), 1887
milestones.description: Volterra defined quantities determined by an entire function, extending calculus-of-variations functionals to a general notion.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record dated 1887.
Wikipedia credits Volterra with introducing the general functional concept in 1887.

milestones.note: MacTutor places the idea itself in 1883; the 1887 publication governs.

milestones.label: Functional calculus applied to Hamilton-Jacobi theory
milestones.work: Volterra, c. 1890
milestones.description: He used the calculus of functionals to carry the Hamilton-Jacobi integration theory over to mathematical physics.

evidence.claim: MacTutor dates this to 1890.

milestones.note: The specific paper was not identified.

milestones.label: Hadamard replaces Volterra's term with 'functional'
milestones.work: Hadamard, Lecons sur le calcul des variations, 1910
milestones.description: Hadamard's lectures introduced the word 'functional', which replaced Volterra's earlier terminology.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: Hadamard later introduced the word functional, replacing Volterra's terminology.
Internet Archive record, 1910 edition.

milestones.label: Volterra's Sorbonne course on functions of lines
milestones.work: Volterra, Lecons sur les fonctions de lignes, Gauthier-Villars, 1913
milestones.description: A systematic course (given 1912, edited by Peres) presenting the calculus of functions of lines.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record, 1913.
Internet Archive record, 1913.

milestones.label: Levy extends nonlinear functional theory
milestones.work: Levy, Lecons d'analyse fonctionnelle, 1922
milestones.description: Levy, a student in Hadamard's circle, continued the theory of nonlinear functionals.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record, 1922.
Wikipedia says nonlinear functional theory was continued by Frechet and Levy.

milestones.label: Volterra's Theory of Functionals (English edition)
milestones.work: Volterra, Theory of Functionals and of Integral and Integro-Differential Equations, Blackie, 1930
milestones.description: Volterra's own summary of the theory of functionals, edited by Fantappie and translated into English.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record, 1930.
Internet Archive record dated 1930.

milestones.note: An earlier systematic account is the 1913 Sorbonne course.

Theory of Functionals

Volterra dated 1887 (publication) vs 1883 (MacTutor idea date). Levy's biography page was not fetched, so biographyUrl is null and his lifespan comes from general knowledge.

milestones.label: Operator methods for differential equations (Carmichael, Boole)
milestones.work: Carmichael 1855; Boole, Treatise on Differential Equations, 1859
milestones.description: British and Irish mathematicians wrote treatises applying operator symbols to differential equations decades before Heaviside.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia's history lists treatises by Carmichael (1855) and Boole (1859) on operator methods.

milestones.note: Wikipedia traces the idea back to Leibniz, Arbogast and Servois.

milestones.label: Heaviside's operators for telegraph and circuit equations
milestones.work: Heaviside, articles in The Electrician, 1880s
milestones.description: Heaviside replaced d/dx by an algebraic variable p to turn circuit differential equations into algebraic ones.

evidence.claim: MacTutor says his operational calculus was developed between 1880 and 1887 to solve circuit differential equations.

milestones.note: Range from a biography; individual article dates in The Electrician were not verified. Reclassified from first_application to precursor: it predates this event's first statement (1892) and belongs to the wider field.

milestones.label: Heaviside's Electrical Papers
milestones.work: Heaviside, Electrical Papers, vol. 1, 1892
milestones.description: The collected papers, whose first volume appeared in 1892, put his operator methods into book form.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive record of Electrical Papers, 1892.

milestones.note: That operator methods appear in these volumes is taken from MacTutor's dating; contents were not read.

milestones.label: Heaviside: On operators in physical mathematics, Part I
milestones.work: Heaviside, Proc. R. Soc. 52, 1893
milestones.description: An explicit public exposition of the operator method in the Royal Society's Proceedings.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Proc. Roy. Soc. London 52, 1893.
zbMATH lists 'On operators in physical mathematics', 1893.
Wikipedia says the method was fully developed by Heaviside in 1893.

milestones.note: MacTutor reports one operational-calculus paper was rejected by the Royal Society referee.

milestones.label: Bromwich ties Heaviside's calculus to contour integrals
milestones.work: Bromwich, Normal coordinates in dynamical systems, Proc. London Math. Soc. (2) 15, 1917
milestones.description: Bromwich put the operator rules on a rigorous footing using contour integrals, which links them to the Laplace transform.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Proc. London Math. Soc. s2-15, 1917.
MacTutor: he put Heaviside's calculus on a rigorous basis, treating operators as contour integrals.

milestones.note: The sources name Bromwich's work but not this title; that this paper carries the justification follows standard accounts and should be double-checked. Some sources date it 1916.

milestones.label: Wiener's operational calculus
milestones.work: Wiener, The operational calculus, Math. Ann. 95, 1926
milestones.description: Wiener analysed the logical status of the calculus and justified it with Fourier-transform methods.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Math. Annalen 95, 1926.
Wikipedia credits Wiener's 1926 review with laying foundations and a Fourier-transform justification.

milestones.label: Jeffreys' Operational Methods in Mathematical Physics
milestones.work: Jeffreys, Operational Methods in Mathematical Physics, Cambridge Tract, 1927
milestones.description: A textbook-level exposition of Heaviside's operators via Laplace-transform methods.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record, 1927.
Wikipedia cites Jeffreys' book for a detailed exposition.

milestones.note: Carson's 1926 survey 'The Heaviside operational calculus' (Bull. AMS, zbMATH 2586813) is nearly contemporary.

milestones.label: Mikusinski's algebraic operational calculus
milestones.work: Mikusinski, Sur les fondements du calcul operatoire, Studia Math. 11, 1950
milestones.description: Mikusinski built the calculus algebraically as a field of convolution quotients, with no appeal to transforms.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Studia Mathematica 11, 1950.
Wikipedia credits Mikusinski with an algebraic approach in the 1930s.

milestones.note: Wikipedia says 1930s; the earliest paper confirmed here is 1950.

works.citation: Electrical Papers, vol. 1
On operators in physical mathematics, Part I, Proc. R. Soc. 52
Normal coordinates in dynamical systems
The operational calculus, Math. Ann. 95
Operational Methods in Mathematical Physics
Sur les fondements du calcul operatoire

notes: Biography URLs for Wiener, Jeffreys and Mikusinski are null (those biographies were not fetched); lifespans for them come from general knowledge, not from a page read here. The summary's 'later justified through Laplace transforms' matches Wikipedia/MacTutor (Bromwich). Carson's 1917 Physical Review paper (10.1103/PhysRev.10.217) and Carson's engineering role (Wikipedia: engineering transients after 1910) are candidates not promoted. Naming: no dated coinage of 'operational calculus' found. No institution milestone found.

milestones.label: Grassmann: arithmetic from successor and induction
milestones.work: Grassmann, Lehrbuch der Arithmetik (early 1860s)
milestones.description: Grassmann showed in the 1860s that many arithmetic facts follow from the successor operation and induction.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia credits Grassmann's 1860s work with showing arithmetic derives from successor and induction.

milestones.note: Decade only; the exact publication year was not verified here.

milestones.label: Peirce's axiomatization of natural-number arithmetic
milestones.work: Peirce, On the Logic of Number, Amer. J. Math. 4, 1881
milestones.description: Peirce gave an early axiomatization of the natural numbers.

evidence.claim: Crossref: American Journal of Mathematics 4, 1881.
Wikipedia says Peirce axiomatized natural-number arithmetic in 1881.

milestones.note: Kept as a precursor because the event is defined by Dedekind and Peano; whether Peirce counts as the first statement is a priority question left open.

milestones.label: Dedekind: Was sind und was sollen die Zahlen
milestones.work: Dedekind, Was sind und was sollen die Zahlen?, Vieweg, 1888
milestones.description: Dedekind characterized the natural numbers by a simply infinite system with a successor map and induction.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia says Dedekind proposed an axiomatization of natural-number arithmetic in 1888.
MacTutor cites Was sind und was sollen die Zahlen? as 1888.
zbMATH 20.0049.05: Dedekind, 'Was sind und was sollen die Zahlen?', Braunschweig 1888.

milestones.note: No bibliographic record for the 1888 first edition was found (Internet Archive lists an 1893 reprint, zbMATH a 1905 edition), so the year rests on history pages.

milestones.label: Peano: Arithmetices principia, nova methodo exposita
milestones.work: Peano, Arithmetices principia, nova methodo exposita, Turin, 1889
milestones.description: Peano restated the axioms in a formal logical notation, the version that carries his name.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record dated 1889.
Internet Archive record dated 1889.
MacTutor calls the pamphlet a landmark in logic and foundations.
zbMATH 21.0051.02: Peano, 'Arithmetices principia, nova methodo exposita', Torino 1889.

milestones.note: Wikipedia notes Peano's simplified version followed Dedekind's; the logical notation also gave the symbol for set membership.

milestones.label: Ingraham titles a paper on Peano's postulates
milestones.work: Ingraham, M. H., A modification of Peano's postulates for positive integers, 1922
milestones.description: Earliest zbMATH title found using the Peano postulates name.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record: title "A modification of Peano's postulates for positive integers", Ingraham, 1922

milestones.note: Title uses the postulates name with a possessive form; not the field name "Peano arithmetic". No earlier title found in 1889-1960 search.

milestones.label: Landau publishes a full development of the number systems from axioms
milestones.work: Landau, E., Grundlagen der Analysis, 1930
milestones.description: Monograph developing the natural numbers and larger systems from axioms in the Peano style.

evidence.claim: Open Library lists the book with first publication year 1930

milestones.note: Chosen as a monograph on axiomatic number systems; Peano's own 1889 treatise is already in the record as a first statement, and Peano 1895 Formulaire not checked.

milestones.label: Goedel's incompleteness theorems for an arithmetic system
milestones.work: Goedel, Ueber formal unentscheidbare Saetze der Principia Mathematica und verwandter Systeme I, Monatsh. Math. Phys. 38, 1931
milestones.description: Goedel proved that a formal arithmetic system of this kind is incomplete, making Peano-style axioms the central object of metamathematics.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Monatshefte fuer Mathematik und Physik 38, 1931.
Wikipedia says the axioms were used in metamathematical research on consistency and completeness.

milestones.note: Goedel's system is built on Peano-style axioms within a type theory; the step from this to first-order PA is later work.

milestones.label: Gentzen's consistency proof for arithmetic
milestones.work: Gentzen, Die Widerspruchsfreiheit der reinen Zahlentheorie, Math. Ann. 112, 1936
milestones.description: Gentzen proved the consistency of first-order arithmetic using transfinite induction.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Mathematische Annalen 112, 1936.

Lehrbuch der Arithmetik

notes: Open: who coined 'Peano axioms' / 'Peano arithmetic' (and when 'Dedekind-Peano') was not found, so there is no naming milestone, and no consolidation/institution milestone was established; derived institutional date is therefore null. Dedekind's priority (1888) over Peano (1889) is a history-page date; Dedekind's ideas predate publication but no dated private source was checked. The Grassmann entry is a decade-level lead. Peano's own 1891 'Sul concetto di numero' (zbMATH 2686871) was not read and is left out. First-order Peano arithmetic as a distinct system (Skolem and later) is not dated here. Fix pass 2: zbMATH confirms Dedekind (1888) and Peano (1889); the coinage of 'Peano axioms' was not found in these records, so no naming milestone was added.

milestones.label: Killing's Programmschrift introduces Lie algebras
milestones.work: Killing, Programmschrift, Lyceum Hosianum, Braunsberg, 1884
milestones.description: In a school programme Killing independently introduced Lie algebras while studying space forms; the classification aim came later.

evidence.claim: MacTutor says he introduced Lie algebras in this 1884 Programmschrift but was not yet aiming at a classification.

milestones.note: Killing's independent discovery of Lie algebras around 1880 is also noted on Wikipedia; this is a local publication, not the classification itself.

milestones.label: Killing: Die Zusammensetzung der stetigen endlichen Transformationsgruppen
milestones.work: Killing, Math. Ann. 31, 33, 34, 36 (four parts), 1888-1890
milestones.description: Killing classified the complex simple Lie algebras into four families and exceptional cases, introducing Cartan subalgebras, the Cartan matrix and root systems.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Part I, Math. Annalen 31, 1888.
Crossref: Part IV, Math. Annalen 36, 1890.
MacTutor describes the classification in these four parts, 1888-1890.
Wikipedia: Killing essentially classified the complex simple Lie algebras in 1888-1890, with unproven but true conjectures.

milestones.note: Wikipedia notes Killing's arguments were less rigorous than Lie's; Crossref dates part II to 1888 although the volume is usually cited as 1889.

milestones.label: Cartan's thesis rigorously completes the classification
milestones.work: Cartan, Sur la structure des groupes de transformations finis et continus, Paris thesis, 1894
milestones.description: Cartan rewrote Killing's results rigorously, corrected gaps and completed the list, including the exceptional algebras.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record: Cartan's 1894 thesis.
MacTutor: Cartan set out to complete Killing's classification in his 1894 thesis.
Wikipedia: Cartan's 1894 dissertation was essentially a rigorous rewriting of Killing's paper.

milestones.note: A preparatory note appeared in 1893 (zbMATH 2681685).

milestones.label: Cartan classifies irreducible representations using the roots
milestones.work: Cartan, Les groupes projectifs qui ne laissent invariante aucune multiplicite plane, Bull. Soc. Math. France 41, 1913
milestones.description: Cartan used the root and weight structure of Killing's classification to describe the irreducible representations of simple groups.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Bulletin de la Societe Mathematique de France, 1913.

milestones.note: That this paper is the first use of the classification for representations rests on general knowledge, not a page read here; other earlier uses were not searched.

milestones.label: van der Waerden's algebraic reproof of the classification
milestones.work: van der Waerden, Die Klassifikation der einfachen Lieschen Gruppen, Math. Z. 37, 1933
milestones.description: A reworked, algebraically cleaner derivation of the classification.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Mathematische Zeitschrift 37, 1933.

milestones.label: The term 'Killing form' appears
milestones.work: Borel, report for Seminaire Bourbaki, 1951 (per Borel 2001)
milestones.description: The name 'Killing form' for the trace form of the adjoint representation first appeared in a 1951 Bourbaki seminar report, a misnomer since Cartan had used the form earlier.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia, citing Borel's historical survey (2001), dates the first use of the term to 1951.

milestones.note: This names the form, not the classification as a whole; no coinage of 'Cartan-Killing classification' was found.

milestones.label: Jacobson's Lie Algebras
milestones.work: Jacobson, Lie algebras, Interscience, 1962
milestones.description: A textbook giving the classification of simple Lie algebras in the algebraic setting.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record: Jacobson, Lie algebras, 1962.

milestones.note: Earlier systematic treatments (for example Weyl 1925-26 or Cartan's own 1933 second edition of the thesis) may exist.

milestones.label: Minkowski's unpublished lecture on spatial intuition and minima of quadratic forms
milestones.work: Minkowski, Raeumliche Anschauung und Minima positiv definiter quadratischer Formen (lecture; published 1991)
milestones.description: A lecture, unpublished until 1991, already contained an early instance of the method later called the geometry of numbers.

evidence.claim: MacTutor, quoting Dieudonne: it contains the first example of the method later developed as the geometry of numbers.

milestones.note: The year 1887 is inferred from MacTutor placing this lecture in the Bonn habilitation context; it is not stated outright.

milestones.label: Minkowski: Geometrie der Zahlen (first instalment)
milestones.work: Minkowski, Geometrie der Zahlen, Teubner, Leipzig, 1896 (completed 1910)
milestones.description: Minkowski presented lattice points in convex bodies, with the first and second theorems, as a geometric method for number theory.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia: in 1896 he presented his geometry of numbers.
Wikipedia attributes the founding of the line of research to Minkowski's work of that name.

milestones.note: Only the completed 1910 edition has a bibliographic record in the sources searched; the 1896 date for the first instalment comes from history pages.

milestones.label: The title 'Geometrie der Zahlen'
milestones.work: Minkowski, Geometrie der Zahlen, 1896
milestones.description: The field's name is the title of Minkowski's book.

evidence.claim: Wikipedia says the term arose from Minkowski's embedding of numbers in higher-dimensional space and his book of that name.

milestones.note: Same work as the first_statement milestone; it genuinely plays both roles.

milestones.label: Minkowski: Diophantische Approximationen
milestones.work: Minkowski, Diophantische Approximationen, Teubner, 1907
milestones.description: An elementary account linking the geometry of numbers to Diophantine approximation and algebraic numbers.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive record dated 1907.
MacTutor: the 1907 book gave an elementary account of this work and its applications to Diophantine approximation and algebraic numbers.

milestones.label: Geometrie der Zahlen, completed edition
milestones.work: Minkowski, Geometrie der Zahlen, Teubner, 1910
milestones.description: The completed book edition collecting the instalments, issued after Minkowski's death in 1909.

evidence.claim: Internet Archive record of the 1910 edition.
Wikipedia cites the 1910 Teubner edition.

milestones.label: Cassels: An Introduction to the Geometry of Numbers
milestones.work: Cassels, An Introduction to the Geometry of Numbers, Springer, 1959
milestones.description: A modern systematic monograph on the subject after the 1930-1960 growth of research.

evidence.claim: zbMATH record: Cassels, 1959.
Wikipedia cites Cassels and describes 1930-1960 research by Mordell, Davenport and Siegel.

milestones.note: Hancock's 1939 history 'Development of the Minkowski Geometry of Numbers' (Internet Archive) is an earlier survey.

Not established: the exact year of first public statement (a series of notes in the early 1890s may precede the 1896 book), the first application to class-number finiteness (Wikipedia credits geometry of numbers with the first proof the ideal class group is finite but gives no year), and an MSC institution milestone (code 11H not verified; the zbMATH classification page could not be read). canonicalName: Commutative algebra from invariant theory and ideals

milestones.label: Dedekind's ideals and modules
milestones.work: Dedekind, supplement to Dirichlet's Vorlesungen ueber Zahlentheorie, 1871 onward
milestones.description: Dedekind defined ideals and the word module for rings of algebraic integers, the number-theoretic root of the subject.

evidence.claim: MacTutor: Dedekind defined an ideal and introduced the word module in 1871.
zbMATH lists the 1879 third edition edited by Dedekind.

milestones.note: Wikipedia says the subject, first called ideal theory, began with Dedekind's work building on Kummer and Kronecker.

milestones.label: Hilbert: Ueber die Theorie der algebraischen Formen
milestones.work: Hilbert, Math. Ann. 36, 1890
milestones.description: Hilbert proved the finite generation of invariants and ideals of polynomials by a non-constructive argument, replacing explicit computation.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Mathematische Annalen 36, pp. 473-534, 1890.
Wikipedia: Hilbert introduced a more abstract approach, replacing computational methods of classical invariant theory.
Crossref: Hilbert, 'Ueber die Theorie der algebraischen Formen', Math. Ann. 36 (1890), pp. 473-534.

milestones.note: MacTutor dates the basis theorem to 1893 (the later paper); the 1890 date for the basis theorem rests on this memoir's content, which was not read here.

milestones.label: Hilbert: Ueber die vollen Invariantensysteme
milestones.work: Hilbert, Math. Ann. 42, 1893
milestones.description: Hilbert's second memoir on invariants, completing the finiteness theory for polynomial ideals.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Mathematische Annalen 42, pp. 313-373, 1893.
MacTutor dates Hilbert's basis theorem to 1893 and notes Gordan's reaction to it.

milestones.note: Dates of the basis theorem and the Nullstellensatz between the two memoirs are a labelling question left open.

milestones.label: Lasker: primary decomposition in polynomial rings
milestones.work: Lasker, Zur Theorie der Moduln und Ideale, Math. Ann. 60, 1905
milestones.description: Lasker introduced primary ideals and proved that ideals in polynomial rings decompose into them.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Mathematische Annalen 60, 1905.
MacTutor: primary ideals were introduced in 1905 by Lasker in polynomial rings.

milestones.label: Noether: Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen
milestones.work: Noether, Math. Ann. 83, 1921
milestones.description: Noether proved primary decomposition for any commutative ring with the ascending chain condition, unifying polynomial rings and rings of numbers.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Mathematische Annalen 83, 1921.
MacTutor: this 1921 paper gave the decomposition in any commutative ring with ascending chain condition.

milestones.label: Krull: Idealtheorie in Ringen ohne Endlichkeitsbedingung
milestones.work: Krull, Math. Ann. 101, 1929
milestones.description: Krull extended abstract ideal theory beyond the chain-condition setting.

evidence.claim: Crossref: Mathematische Annalen 101, 1929.
MacTutor: the axiomatic treatment of commutative rings was developed in the 1920s by Noether and Krull.

milestones.label: van der Waerden: Moderne Algebra

milestones.label: Weldon applies correlation to biological populations
milestones.work: Weldon, Certain correlated variations in Crangon vulgaris, Proc. R. Soc. 51, 1892
